---
title: "Example 10: Parallel iteration with `in_parallel()`"
engine: knitr
---

```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(socviz)
```

## Load our packages

```{r}
#| label: "10-example-01"
#| message: TRUE
library(here)      # manage file paths
library(socviz)    # data and some useful functions
library(tidyverse) # your friend and mine
library(mirai)     # parallel workers for purrr
```

## A slow task

A bootstrap draws many random samples from the data, with replacement. It then
calculates the same statistic on each sample. Each sample is independent of the
others, so the task is easy to divide among several processes.

This function draws one bootstrap sample from `organdata`. It fits a model of
the donor rate on consent law and returns the coefficient for presumed consent.
The `Sys.sleep()` call adds a quarter of a second, to make the function slow.

```{r}
#| label: "10-example-02"
boot_coef <- function(i, data) {
  boot_sample <- dplyr::slice_sample(data, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)
  fit <- stats::lm(donors ~ consent_law, data = boot_sample)
  Sys.sleep(0.25)
  tibble::tibble(rep = i, estimate = stats::coef(fit)[["consent_lawPresumed"]])
}

boot_coef(1, organdata)
```

The function refers to package functions with `::`, for example
`dplyr::slice_sample()`. The parallel workers do not automatically load our
packages. The `::` prefix tells each worker where to find the function.

## Run it sequentially

First, we run 24 replicates with an ordinary `map()`. Each replicate takes at
least 0.25 seconds, so this takes at least six seconds.

```{r}
#| label: "10-example-03"
system.time(
  seq_out <- map(1:24, \(i) boot_coef(i, organdata)) |>
    list_rbind()
)
```

## Start the workers

`daemons()` from the `mirai` package starts a set of background R processes.
These processes are the workers. Do not start more workers than the number of
cores in your computer. Here we use four workers, or fewer if the computer has
fewer cores.

The `seed` argument makes the random numbers in the workers reproducible.

```{r}
#| label: "10-example-04"
n_workers <- min(4, parallel::detectCores() - 1)

daemons(n_workers, seed = 1234)

status()$connections
```

## Which process does the work?

`Sys.getpid()` returns the ID number of the R process that runs it. In an
ordinary `map()`, each call runs in our own R session. So each call returns the
same number.

```{r}
#| label: "10-example-05"
map_int(1:8, \(x) Sys.getpid()) |>
  unique()
```

When we put the function inside `in_parallel()`, `purrr` sends each call to a
worker. Each call can return a different number.

```{r}
#| label: "10-example-06"
map_int(1:8, in_parallel(\(x) Sys.getpid())) |>
  unique()
```

## Run it in parallel

Next, we run the bootstrap with `in_parallel()`. The workers do not see the
objects in our session. So we must give them each object that the function
needs. Here, the function needs `boot_coef()` and `organdata`. We supply them
as named arguments to `in_parallel()`.

```{r}
#| label: "10-example-07"
system.time(
  par_out <- map(
    1:24,
    in_parallel(
      \(i) boot_coef(i, organdata),
      boot_coef = boot_coef,
      organdata = organdata
    )
  ) |>
    list_rbind()
)
```

The time is approximately the sequential time divided by the number of workers.
There's some overhead. Each worker must also start and receive the data, so the
gain is a little smaller than that.

## A common error

If we do not supply an object, the workers cannot find it. The map stops with
an error.

```{r}
#| label: "10-example-08"
#| error: TRUE
map(1:4, in_parallel(\(i) boot_coef(i, organdata)))
```

## Look at the results

The parallel version gives one row per replicate, the same as the sequential
version. The random samples are different, so the estimates are different.
They have approximately the same distribution.

```{r}
#| label: "10-example-09"
bind_rows(
  Sequential = seq_out,
  Parallel = par_out,
  .id = "method"
) |>
  summarize(
    mean = mean(estimate),
    sd = sd(estimate),
    .by = method
  )
```

## Stop the workers

When the parallel work is complete, stop the workers. This releases the
processes and their memory.

```{r}
#| label: "10-example-10"
daemons(0)
```

If you do not call `daemons()` first, `in_parallel()` has no workers to use.
In that case `map()` runs each call in your own session, one at a time. This is
nice because it means the same code can run in parallel or serially (e.g. on
different machines).
